A leaderboard says model A scores eighty five percent, and model B scores eighty four.
Is that a difference, or noise?
We asked three models the same one hundred questions from one video benchmark: how many times did the person do something.
Three options each, so guessing gets thirty three percent.
Opus five point five: fifty two percent. Sonnet five point five: forty eight. Haiku four point five: forty four.
Now the error bars. Ninety five percent Wilson intervals, each about ten points wide on either side.
They overlap heavily. Every pair is tied: p of point five six, point six four, and point two eight.
Tied means the data cannot tell them apart. It does not mean they are identical.
Ten paired tests in all, and none survives a Bonferroni correction.
How many items would it take to call these gaps? These are estimates.
The eight point gap needs about five hundred ten items. The four point gaps need about twelve hundred seventy, and about two thousand sixty.
The whole task has two hundred. It cannot rank these models at these gaps.
Now, what the number hides. The right answer sits in the middle on thirty five of the hundred items.
Haiku picks the middle fifty nine times.
When the right answer is B, Haiku scores seventy four percent. At A, twenty three. At C, thirty three.
At default temperature it still picks the middle fifty five times, so greedy decoding is not the cause.
The shuffle test: move the options under the same letters, and ask again.
Here is one item. The content moves. The pick stays on B.
On the sixty two items where Haiku's chosen option moved, it followed the answer twenty eight times, stayed on the same letter twenty eight times, and switched to the third option six times.
Sonnet followed the answer on fifty six of sixty four moved items, and two separate runs agreed on ninety three of one hundred answers.
Opus followed the answer on forty of sixty four, with no position preference: thirteen same letter against eleven third option, p of point four two.
Similar scores. Very different behavior.
One more result, and a fragile one. Labelling the options one, two, three instead of A, B, C dropped Haiku from forty four to thirty five percent, p of point zero two two.
One item flipping makes that a tie, p of point zero nine two.
It is still real. Haiku repeated all one hundred answers exactly, so the gap is not sampling noise. It is too small for one hundred items to pin down.
So before trusting model A beats model B by N points, ask three questions.
What are the intervals?
How many items would a gap that size need?
Does the score survive shuffling the options?
This repo answers all three, for any model, on any MVBench slice.
